2. by analysis and synthesis.

## Proof by Contraposition

Proof by contraposition is useful when you want to prove implications. It aims to answer a question of the type: "Show that $\mathbf{A} \Rightarrow \mathbf{B}$. "

It simply involves showing another implication than the one requested, namely the implication " $($ not $B) \Rightarrow($ not $A) »$. Indeed, using a truth table, it is easily observed that the two properties " $A \Rightarrow B$ " and " $($ not $B) \Rightarrow($ not $A) »$ are equivalent:

| $\mathbf{A}$ | $\mathbf{0}$ | $\mathbf{0}$ | $\mathbf{1}$ | $\mathbf{1}$ |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| $\mathbf{B}$ | $\mathbf{0}$ | $\mathbf{1}$ | $\mathbf{0}$ | $\mathbf{1}$ |
| $\mathrm{A} \Rightarrow \mathrm{B}$ | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| $\neg \mathrm{A}$ | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| $\neg \mathrm{B}$ | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| $(\neg \mathrm{B}) \Rightarrow(\neg \mathrm{A})$ | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1 |

## Proof by Contradiction

Proof by contradiction is based on the principle of the excluded middle: a property A is either true or false. Proof by contradiction aims to answer a question of the type: "Show that the property A is false."

It involves assuming that the property A is true, and then, under this assumption, arriving at an absurdity. In other words, it is a matter of finding properties $\mathrm{P}_{1}, \mathrm{P}_{2}, \ldots, \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{k}}$ such that $A \Rightarrow P_{1} \Rightarrow P_{2} \Rightarrow \cdots \Rightarrow P_{k}$, where $P_{k}$ is a property that is notoriously false. We then deduce that the property A could not have been true and, since it is necessarily either true or false, it is false.

In particular, whenever one wishes to show that a property A is false, one can always assume, without loss of generality, that A is true. Indeed, in life, there are two scenarios: either the property A is false, in which case we have already won; or it is true, and this is the only interesting case, so the case in which we decide to place ourselves.

However, note that many readers tend to consider the use of proof by contradiction as rather cumbersome: if one can show directly that A is false, why bother first assuming that $\mathrm{A}$ is true, and thus burdening oneself with an unnecessary assumption? In general, indeed, the simpler a proof is, the better it will be understood, and the happier its author will be.

Finally, note that proof by contradiction is a special case of proof by contraposition: indeed, to show the property "not A" - that is, the property "True $\Rightarrow($ not $A) »$ - one has in fact shown the property " $\mathrm{A} \Rightarrow$ False".

\[
